title: How much would you realistically pay for a 3D RPG that teaches you a language?
author: OkraSuper9329
selftext:
I'm developing a game called VocaBound using Claude and Unreal Engine.

It's a 3D RPG where you move to Taiwan with very little money and have to build a life for yourself. You find work, earn money, explore realistic neighborhoods, talk to people, and learn Mandarin through everyday situations.

The idea is to make something that feels like an actual game rather than a language learning app. You learn because you need to communicate and accomplish things in the world.

It's still early in development, but we're hoping to eventually have multiple detailed neighborhoods, different jobs, activities, stories, and an adaptive language learning system that works for beginners and more advanced learners.

I'm trying to figure out what would be a reasonable price for the finished game.

Would $70 be completely unreasonable? Would you pay $15, $30, $50, or more for something like this?

I'm genuinely curious how other developers would price it.

comments.author: ichivictus
comments.body: Would this be something that uses claude api directly in game? A subscription model would make sense to me I think. Really cool idea though.

replies.author: OkraSuper9329
replies.body:
We're using Claude to help develop the game, but we're hoping to keep most of the actual gameplay and language learning systems working without needing constant API calls. We want people to be able to play offline too.

We're leaning more toward a one-time purchase because I personally don't really like subscriptions, but we're still figuring out what makes the most sense with the development and ongoing costs. Do you think having AI-powered conversations would make a subscription more worthwhile?

replies.author: ichivictus
replies.body:
Yeah if it is offline and local then one time purchase makes sense.

But I personally would feel like the quality won't be that good for learning. Voice recognition might work a bit but having an actual ai model check for tonal, pitch, grammar, slang etc. would be very useful for learning and feel more natural possibly.

I was imagining something like this in game, I go into a restaraunt and say "could I order combo one?" And then the waitress would say "I see what you mean. But you pronounce combo like this... com-bo."

Idk if that makes sense but just my 2 cents.

replies.author: OkraSuper9329
replies.body:
That makes sense! Your feedback has me considering a combination of the two options. What would you think about a one-time purchase for the offline game, with an optional monthly subscription for more advanced AI features to cover the ongoing costs?

What prices would you consider reasonable for each, or would you rather just have a subscription for everything?

replies.author: ichivictus
replies.body:
I'd consider something like 30 dollars for the base game that includes 5-10 dollars of usage. Then allow player to top up. Add a 20% or so profit on top of the real api cost for topups. Something like that.

But also keep the base game minus the advance ai features when usage is depleted and allow player to disable the ai if they want to save it or not use it at all.

comments.author: teapot_RGB_color
comments.body:
It's incredible difficult to answer. I've built a couple of Vietnamese learning apps now, with and without AI. And I haven't done anything with it.. yet.

The difficult part is adding the language learning part.

I think my first question would be, what vocabulary size are you aiming at (which would give a good indication to CEFR level)

Edit: the range would be from $0 to $200, it depends totally on the execution.

replies.author: OkraSuper9329
replies.body:
Thank you for the detailed response! It's really helpful hearing from someone who has actually worked on something similar.

We have about 12 thousand words in our database right now and want to work someone up from pre-A1 to as close to C2 as possible, even if just with the words and grammar they know. We are following the CEFR levels to help decide which words and grammar to introduce when, while also considering how frequently they're used in natural speech.

I definitely agree that making the learning part effective without turning it into homework is one of the hardest parts. We want learning the language in the game to make the story progress and unlock new things like conversations, jobs, and quests. The idea is that players actually want to learn the language because it helps them accomplish things in the world, rather than just completing exercises to move forward.

We're also trying to make it adaptive to different language levels, so a complete beginner and someone who already knows Mandarin can experience the same world but with different levels of language difficulty and support. We want players to be able to ask for help when they need it, but gradually become more independent as they improve.

For the fatigue issue, we're hoping that mixing language learning with exploration, earning money, decorating your home, minigames, and other activities will give people opportunities to enjoy the game without constantly feeling like they're studying. Of course, we still need to test whether this actually works.

I also agree with your concerns about AI translations, especially with Mandarin being so context dependent. Right now we're using AI quite a bit because of our limited budget, but we don't want to rely on it alone for the final language content. If we can get enough funding, we want native speakers to review the language and hire native voice actors as well.

We don't expect VocaBound to be the only source of language learning someone uses, but we do hope it can help quite a bit on its own. Eventually we'd also love to get it into classrooms to make school language programs more exciting for students.

I'm curious, when you were working on your Vietnamese apps, did you find anything that helped keep the learning effective without making it feel too much like homework?

replies.author: teapot_RGB_color
replies.body:
Good reply. Seems like you already put some planning on it.

Reading was the best / easiest way to put less fatigue, having access to directly click words for translation, but I lock the clicks to "unlock keys". I tried linking it to online dictionaries, but I gave up with that because of context sensitive language, and too many translations make it more confusing and less learning (Linq does mistake here). So instead I manually curated words with the closest English word.

I also marked audiofiles and created a sidecar file with the timings of words to create karaoke effect with highlighting words.

With output (writing), I think only llm can work, because it's impossible to curate all variantsof how you can say something. And marking something as wrong, which is right, shatters the trust in the app completely.
But with that also comes the issue with token limit and thinking time. I used a fast gate model with a one token output to decide if it should be using a thinking model or a fast model. Because only using a thinking model would kill my token budget, and trying local llm would go up to 30 second before responding. I found gemini to be the one of the fastest ones with an "acceptable" budget, cloude and gpt got expensive fast.

comments.author: hlopez137
comments.body:
If it lacks mechanics that are backed by actual linguistic learning research I’d want to pay very little, if anything. More than $5 and I’d start questioning the value proposition 

There’s so many language learning tools and games available, and honestly your biggest competitor nowadays is probably LLMs themselves. 

The only thing that’d make me choose paying for a game over an LLM for *actual* learning is a structure backed by science, researchers, trustworthy names.

replies.author: OkraSuper9329
replies.body:
I actually agree with this! I don't want VocaBound to just be a fun game that throws random vocabulary at you and calls itself educational.

We're trying to build the learning system around second language acquisition research, including comprehensible input, spaced repetition, contextual learning, and adaptive support. The idea is that instead of memorizing a list of words, you're using them to accomplish things in the game, and the game gradually expects you to become more independent with the language.

We also hope to work with language teachers and eventually get VocaBound into classrooms. We're still early in development though, so we definitely need to test how effective the learning actually is rather than just assuming it works.

I think your point about competing with LLMs is really interesting too. What would a game have to offer that would make you choose it over practicing with something like ChatGPT?

replies.author: hlopez137
replies.body:
Then I think that’s awesome and that’d be the main selling point you should market tbh, endorsements by actual teachers, professionals, or researchers I think will be the differentiator

Your question about what would make a game my first choice over an LLM - what I struggle with is getting the LLM to pick topics that have variety. My personal Gemini pulls a LOT from previous convos, interests etc and ends up recycling and hyperfocusing on such a small set of material. That + I don’t have a good feel for “is this extremely formal rigid language that it’s reinforcing with me or a more usable everyday language with slang?” 

If I knew I’d get varied practice topics, a choice of everyday or more rigid language, and it’s easy to just pick up for 5-10min stretches and then drop without too much friction, then that’d capture my personal wants

replies.author: OkraSuper9329
replies.body: Thank you! You brought up some really good points, especially about learning natural speech and being able to play for shorter periods of time. I really appreciate the feedback! We're still figuring a lot of this out, so it's helpful to hear what people would actually want from the game.

comments.author: FosterTheSpookyGhost
comments.body: As an expat actually living in Taiwan, I think it’s a great idea! $50-70 as a one-time purchase, sure, but if it’s a subscription then probably only like $10/month.

replies.author: OkraSuper9329
replies.body:
Thank you!! That's really encouraging, especially coming from someone actually living in Taiwan! I studied there for three months and that's actually where the idea came from. We really want to recreate the feeling of living there and having a reason to use Mandarin every day.

We're leaning toward a one-time purchase rather than a subscription. I'm curious, since you live in Taiwan, what are some everyday experiences you think would be important to include to make it feel authentic?

comments.author: rrcecil
comments.body:
I have thought about this. Like tired of Duolingo and all those others. I thought a Roguelite would be a good example, but also something long form where you are kinda maybe like someone who washed up on the shores of a foreign country and part of the progression is like getting immersed with the town or something and to progress you have to be able to communicate. Then maybe the second half is more RPG. 

Word vomit but I do think there is a virtually unexplored niche here and a lot of different directions. Like you need a specific skill set and to be bilingual but I feel like the barrier to entry is so much lower now that this is feasible now. 

I’d def shoot around some ideas on this

replies.author: OkraSuper9329
replies.body:
That's actually really close to what we're trying to do! You arrive in Taiwan with very little money and have to figure out how to build a life for yourself. You start with basic conversations and jobs, but as your language improves you can unlock more opportunities, explore new places, and get involved in more complicated stories.

I really want the player to feel like they're actually living in Taiwan rather than just doing language exercises with a game around them. I studied there for three months and having real reasons to communicate made learning so much more enjoyable for me.

I'd love to hear more of your ideas! Especially about how to make the RPG side fun enough that people would want to play even when they're not specifically trying to study.

comments.author: ffxivthrowaway03
comments.body: Realistically?  You're not an AAA dev or even an AA dev so your price point caps out at around $30 USD regardless of what you made.  That's just where the indie games market has more or less settled over the years.

replies.author: OkraSuper9329
replies.body:
That's a fair point! We're still pretty early in development and definitely don't have the resources of a AAA studio. We're trying to figure out how people would value something that's both a game and a language learning resource.

I was thinking people might compare it to other indie RPGs, but also to language learning programs that can cost quite a bit more. I don't want to overprice it just because it's educational though.

Do you think $30 would still be your ceiling if it had a substantial amount of gameplay and could help someone learn Mandarin over hundreds of hours?
